The disbursements were directed to projects on infrastructure, blood supply, and obstetrics and gynaecology. It was also the only beneficiary of GFATM, which disbursed $5 million for surgical infrastructure in 2014 and 2015. ECA, supported by the EU and CEDB, focused on infrastructure and paediatric surgery with a total of $65.7 million. EAP, which received 84.6% of its total $44.4 million from ADB, focused on projects on infrastructure and blood supply systems. South Asia, 71% financed by ADB, with 15% from IDA from a total of $34.7 million, had projects on infrastructure, obstetrics and gynaecology, and orthopaedics and trauma surgery.26

Multilateral organisations directed 78% of disbursements towards surgical system strengthening projects, building infrastructure ($355 million), and blood supply systems ($45.4 million), both led by RDBs and the EU. Orthopaedics and trauma care with $76.7 million led by the UN System, paediatric surgery with $17.5 million led by CEDB and obstetrics and gynaecology $5.9 million led by the EU make up the top three funded single-specialty programmes. Anaesthesia and critical care, on the other hand, was the least funded specialty programme with $400 000.26

The IBRD/IDA disbursed a total of $374.81 million from 2014 to 2022 to surgical care delivery and system strengthening in Ukraine, India and El Salvador and multi-country implementation in Africa. Project details included strengthening management of NCDs and injuries, improving outpatient-based procedures and day surgeries, improving the prevention, early detection and treatment of cervical cancer, to strengthen capacity for collecting, analysing and sharing data on cancers through cancer registries, and to improve cancer management (online supplemental appendix III).19

This brings the total sum of multilateral disbursement to $901.5 million amounting to 0.4% of total multilateral DAH. During the study period, RDBs contributed 2.5% of their total health allocation to surgical care. The WBG disbursed 1% of funds to surgical care, while the EU allocated 0.13%. The UN and vertical funds allocated approximately 0.06% and 0.02% of their disbursements to surgical care, respectively.26

#### Implementation channels and flow types

Flow types are the types of finances provided by development institutions. The UN, EU, GFATM and Arab Fund disbursed 100% of their funds as grants to recipients. WBG, ADB and Arab Bank for Economic Development in Africa provided only loans. IDB, OPEC Fund, CEDB and ISDB provided versatile finances, disbursing in the form of grants, loans or other official flows.26

Multilateral organisations used various implementation channels (online supplemental appendix III). The EU used multilateral organisations in 53% of disbursements, recipient governments in 14% and NGOs (either donor-based/international) for 10% of disbursements. The UN used only multilateral organisations for implementation. Approximately 83% of disbursements from RDBs and 100% from WBG and GFATM were implemented through recipient governments. IsDB disbursed $2.7 million in grants to the private sector in recipient countries. AFESD disbursed in the form of grants and loans to recipient governments and the public sector in the recipient government.26

#### Multilateral organisations and the private sector in low- and middle-income countries

The private sector is a key stakeholder in LMICs in terms of service delivery, medical innovation and financial capital.51 The evaluation of investments from the IFC therefore offers multilateral perspectives for the private sector in LMICs.

In our analysis, we found 26 investment projects from IFC for a total of $1.64 billion to surgical care. Half of these projects were in LMICs amounting to $369.7 million (22.5%) (online supplemental appendix III table ii). The Philippines secured $107 million for infrastructure. India secured $81.3 million for service delivery and health information systems. Companies in MENA secured 37.4% of the investments with projects in Morocco and Egypt securing $80 million service delivery, and those in Pakistan securing investments approximating $47.57 million for surgical infrastructure, service delivery and workforce training. SSA secured $25.4 million (6.8%). When summarised, the system strengthening projects consisted of building facilities for surgical care delivery, expanding workforce training, surgical equipment, and consumables, pharmaceuticals, and diagnostics. Surgical care delivery emphasised ambulatory (day) surgeries, oncologic surgical care, ophthalmology surgery, and orthopaedic surgical services. Around 63% of the investments were in the form of loans; 35% were equity with over $80 million in local currency including a concessional loan structured as blended finance.31

## Discussion

### The trends

Financial contributions from multilateral organisations to surgical care totalled $901.5 million, only 0.4% of total multilateral development assistance for health from 2014 to 2022.26 Changes in global health priorities, such as pandemics and conflicts, influence development assistance,52 and our analysis showed disbursements to surgical care in 2021 dropped by 64% from 2019 values, despite multilateral disbursements doubling to $41 billion in the same time period.14 The year marking the highest multilateral disbursement was also the year with one of the lowest disbursements for surgical projects. This reveals a significant funding imbalance across health domains, potentially driven by the unmatched influence of disease-specific global health initiatives that dominate the multilateral financing architecture.

Disbursements to surgical care went mostly to building surgical infrastructure and blood delivery systems, which parallel the critical infrastructure limitation in LMICs.53 One explanation for this heavy funding focus is that development banks have established expertise in infrastructure development and financing across multiple sectors and therefore more readily finance infrastructure projects in health as well.54 55 Another explanation is that investments in infrastructure offer an easily trackable and measurable outcome compared with investments in service delivery or workforce which have more compound measurement metrics.56 Training human resources in health faces well-documented challenges including high retention failures and delayed impact.57 This misalignment with the banks’ standard metrics could explain tendencies to favour investments in infrastructure projects. National surgical plans may have the potential to counteract this by establishing strategic priorities, robust monitoring and evaluation frameworks, and tangible timelines with measurable outcomes—thereby attracting sustainable finance.9

Despite anaesthesia and critical care being fundamental pillars of any successful surgical system, these essential services remain alarmingly underfunded, receiving less than 0.1% of total surgical system investments.26 When this chronic underinvestment is compounded by the critically low workforce density of anaesthesiologists in LMICs—ranging from just 0.02 to 0.4 providers per 100 000 population6—it demands urgent re-evaluation of investment priorities across surgical systems strengthening initiatives worldwide. Investments will need to be made to address the specialised workforce shortages in LMICs, as it is difficult to improve surgical care provision with less than 10% of the WHO-recommended workforce density.58

### The actors

While vertical funds and the UN were the largest multilateral organisations that contributed to health, disbursement to surgical projects was heavily carried by MDBs, including the WBG. This is visualised in the difference in disbursement to surgical care compared with all health, which ranged from 2.5% to 0.06% across the various multilateral organisations.26 We observe the effect this has on the regional trends of disbursements, where SSA received a major share of the region-specified multilateral support for overall health, while EAP and LAC took the surgical care counterpart. This reflects our thematic analysis findings, which identified equity concerns observed in the vertical multilateral system, that can inadvertently contribute to growing inequalities in access to health services, not only through discordant financial support but also through creating competing impacts on domestic investment priorities.49

The overall trend in financing surgical care and the susceptibility of development assistance to donor priorities has emphasised the need for a domain-based funding that can withstand sudden changes in global health priorities. The establishment of SURGfund,59 modelled on impactful multilateral global health initiatives such as GFATM and GAVI, may be able to replicate their success in ensuring sustainable financing for surgical care. However, given the cross-cutting nature of surgical care, such a design would theoretically not risk creating islands or engendering inequity, which vertical funds have been criticised for.33

Multilateral development banks demonstrated growing capacity to support surgical systems.26 Their expanding co-financing structures increase their financial and regional reach, reflecting their potential to support LMICs regardless of geography. MDBs primarily use recipient governments as the implementing partner, which points to government-led and government-executed programmes. While this supports recipient government agency and avoids the creation of parallel systems typical of vertical funds, it may not directly translate into successful implementation. Implementation efficiency gaps in government run systems persist and could be bridged through systemic engagement of civil society organisations and NGOs.60

Our analysis showed that the AfDB had the lowest engagement in financing surgical care in its region compared with other RDBs and their respective constituents. This has significant implications, as the majority of African countries require external support and have not yet managed to meet the 2001 Abuja Declaration to increase their government health budgeting to 15%.10

This reduced engagement in the region may be a reflection of how LMICs are reluctant to acquire more debt to invest in healthcare because the current form of deficit financing is more suitable for capital rather than recurrent expenditures.61 It may also be a result of the bank country strategies which did not give sufficient focus to the health sector.62 Weak public finances in Africa, and rising debt:GDP ratios exacerbated by the pandemic, also negatively affect African countries’ capacity to access more loans.54 In spite of these, the latest commitment from AfDB to disburse $6 billion in the 6 years from 2025 to 2030 in support of primary healthcare, including surgical care, and pharmaceutical manufacturing development,63 could be evidence of shifting outlook in the region and the opportunities available in development banks to address disparities in surgical care provision on the continent.

### The way forward

#### Aligning with the new global health era

We are witnessing the threat that a narrow funding base and shifting political climate pose to traditionally funded multilateral organisations such as the UN system. The withdrawal of the USA, the largest government donor to multilaterals, and the subsequent decrease in contributions from the UK and other major bilateral donors are uncharted territory.64 LMICs are ill-prepared to independently finance their systems, as demonstrated in their dependence on external support for a significant amount of their healthcare expenditure.10

As the WHO undergoes significant reform that addresses its weaknesses following recent changes in 2025,44 LMICs continue to tread the evolving global health financing landscape. Technical support from multilateral organisations remains as crucial as financial contributions. Using multilateral expertise to support the design of policies and frameworks, such as the NSOAPs, to achieve increased domestic health financing,40 mobilise private sector finance54 and monitor progress in surgical care provision41 would be fundamental to ensure that policies are feasible and can be realistically implemented in the target timeframe. In this regard, the implications for countries to maximise on multilateral support may include the following:

#### Identifying key partners

Sustainable financing requires identifying the right partners who align with LMICs’ surgical systems agenda.

- Multilateral development banks align with LMICs’ transition from aid dependency towards strategic partnerships that prioritise national health system goals. Their programme-based financing and direct use of recipient governments as implementation partners28 foster autonomy. Their versatile financing mechanisms to increase their lending capacity, use of innovative financing, concessionality and multibank co-financing65 provide a rich area for LMICs to finance surgical care. Indonesia’s co-financed Health System Strengthening Project is evidence of this capacity and can be a learning model for other countries.37

- The IHME Financing Global Health 2025 report shows that regional development banks were one of two organisations—the other being the Gates Foundation—which had positive growth in disbursements in 2025,66 making them a sustainable partner amidst shifting health financing landscape.

- Although financial data are not yet robust for SURGfund, early reports also show positive outcomes from a scale-up of locally driven projects. Strategic designing of programmes geared towards addressing surgical care disparities with coordinated government support attracts financing from multiple sources, as demonstrated in the Makueni County Project.59

- Private sector engagement from MDBs, particularly IFC, which offers local currency financing and innovative instruments such as blended finance, is an opportunity for the private sector to engage in surgical system strengthening.31 In times of economic uncertainty and increased debt burden, LMICs are devising strategies to mobilise private sector capital to finance health systems.54 The private sector can take advantage of this unique access to IFC financing to support innovation and surgical service delivery expansion.

#### Establishing financing platforms

AUDA/NEPAD’s African Leadership Meeting(ALM)-driven regional health financing dialogues and the establishment of regional health financing hubs40 are strategic moves that can be potentially adopted to include surgical care financing. Such platforms allow countries to continually assess their financial partners and rapidly respond to changes to prevent the reversal of progress.39 Creation of a surgical financing task force that is responsible for maintaining partnerships, providing monitoring and evaluation on progress, and designing and implementing programmes, along with ministries of health and finance, would increase efficiency and reduce fragmentation in the implementation of surgical projects.39

#### Recognising agency

Innovative multilaterals thrive through partnership with donor governments, philanthropy, financial markets and private organisations, which gives them the capacity to weather unprecedented changes.33 Taking lessons from global health initiatives to look ahead, a robust multilateral engagement will be highly dependent on country-driven initiatives that demonstrate feasibility and tangible return on investment. Countries should take the central role in financing small-scale programmes and generate evidence to engage result-driven external partners, such as philanthropy and global health initiatives.42

Research has demonstrated not only the cost of failing to invest in surgery but also the monetary67 and social gains of investing in surgical care. Surgical, Obstetric, and and Anaethesia (SOA) care is not a competitor for scarce resources; it is a synergistic partner in healthcare delivery that will allow countries to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals and Universal Health Care.68

## Limitations of the study

This study has limitations due to gaps in data tracking allocations to surgical care. Although our paper used the most comprehensive databases that best track and document DAH, allowing for uniform comparison, these databases are incomplete. Both the IHME and OECD lack full donor inclusion, for example, the IHME does not report on IsDB, the WBG disbursements are limited in OECD CRS and there is limited data on non-DAC emerging economies that do not report to the OECD. The provisional and estimated numbers in the OECD, which is updated at least twice a year, may vary at the end of the year once the full report has been finalised. The values in this study are therefore the best estimates available during the time of study. We supplemented these databases with quantitative analysis from multilateral organisation individual databases. ‘Surgery’ or ‘surgical care’ is not categorically reported in any of the databases used. We deliberately left out general terms—such as ‘operative’ and ‘operation’ to reduce false negative results and focused on DAC 3 Sector Codes 120–130 which may exclude some sectors that could potentially contain surgical projects (eg, 720, 730—Emergency response/disaster prevention). As the focus of this study is to quantify development assistance for health, we deemed this decision necessary.

## Conclusion

The pattern of multilateral contributions to surgical systems from 2014 to 2022 has shown that, despite a noticeable growth following the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery, surgical care remains underfunded at 0.4% of multilateral development assistance, compared with the 50% that goes to communicable diseases.25 However, multilateral organisations’ strong operational capacity, structural adaptability and innovative financing mechanisms make them a key player in supporting surgical care improvements globally.14 32

Within surgical systems itself, there exists a disproportionate gap in financing between various building blocks that outline potential perceived risks associated with investments in components such as workforce or service delivery. NSOAPs play a fundamental role in establishing transparency, accountability, and monitoring frameworks to mobilise development bank finance.9

Multilateral development banks have demonstrated their versatility to support surgical system strengthening through primarily recipient government-led programmes and private sector mobilisation.54 Given the substantial role of the private sector in healthcare provision in LMICs, strengthening of the private sector through multilaterals has the potential to create robust opportunities for public-private partnerships and support efforts to increase access to surgical care delivery.

## Abstract

Surgery is an indispensable component of a health system, yet financing its delivery faces significant financing challenges. This study seeks to address the research question: What is the financial contribution of philanthropy to the delivery of surgical care in low and middle-income countries (LMICs)?

This study combines a qualitative and a quantitative component to examine the magnitude of philanthropic contributions in surgical care. The qualitative analysis is composed of a narrative review of peer-reviewed and gray literature that was conducted and synthesised through thematic analysis to identify patterns of philanthropic engagement. To quantify philanthropic contributions, a cross-sectional analysis was employed by using the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development Creditor Reporting System, to identify philanthropic funding for surgical projects between 2014 and 2022.

Four thematic domains were identified from the narrative review: (1) an overview of philanthropy, highlighting its role in filling critical funding gaps in financing health systems; (2) the modes of engagement in philanthropic giving, including partnerships with multilateral organisations, corporate social responsibility, domestic philanthropy, crowdfunding and remittances; (3) recipient channels such as non-profit, non-government organisations, faith-based organisations, non-profit private hospitals and academic institutions who more often contribute to surgical service delivery, research and capacity building; (4) facilitators include flexibility and risk tolerance, contrasted by barriers such as weak policy environments and donor dependency. Quantitatively, 10 philanthropic organisations collectively funded a total of $124.8 million to surgical care from 2014 to 2022. East Asia and the Pacific received the largest share totalling $38.02 million (30.5%). Pediatric surgery received the most amount of funding at $49.07 million (39.3%), with 95.3% contributed by the UBS Optimus Foundation.

Global surgery remains chronically underfunded despite its substantial burden of disease. Amid shifting financial aid landscapes, renewed philanthropic investment in global surgery is urgent. Philanthropy often focuses resources where perceived need is greatest. Although modest in scale, it has the potential to seed and catalyse surgical systems, advancing the expansion of access to surgical care in LMICs.

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Philanthropic investments have the potential to improve surgical care access in low and middle-income countries (LMICs), where financing remains a major challenge despite surgery being a critical global health priority.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- This study provides new insights on the role of philanthropic donors and organisations in the global financing landscape in the realm of surgical care in LMICs, which yields the scale, donor sources and focus areas of philanthropic donors and organisations and their contributions.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- Philanthropic funding, both small and large scale, plays an increasingly vital role in surgical care amid current geopolitical crises. While smaller contributions cover individual surgical costs, larger grants have the potential to catalyse research, capacity building and policy development to strengthen surgical care and integrate essential surgery into health systems.

## Introduction

Surgical care is an indispensable component of a health system. Accounting for an estimated 18%–30% of the global disease burden, surgically treatable conditions disproportionately affect low and middle-income countries (LMICs), where access to surgical care is severely limited.1 Unmet need for surgical, obstetrical and anaesthesia care in LMICs is projected to result in a loss of $12.3 trillion in economic output by 2030.1 Despite the critical role of surgery in achieving Universal Health Coverage (UHC) and several Sustainable Development Goals, surgical care remains underfunded.1 2

Progress towards making surgical care accessible, safe and affordable has been shaped by key milestones.

In 1980, Dr Halfdan Mahler, then Director-General of WHO, emphasised that most of the world lacked access to skilled surgical care.3 In 2015, global surgery gained prominence through the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery (LCoGS) report, the World Health Assembly (WHA) Resolution 68.15 integrating surgical and anaesthesia care into health systems, and the inclusion of essential surgery in Disease Control Priorities.1 4 Following this, the National Surgical, Obstetric, and Anesthesia Plans were developed as strategic frameworks incorporated into national health plans to strengthen surgical systems.5 Building on growing momentum of surgical and anaesthesia care as essential to health systems, recent WHA resolutions (76.2 in 2023 and 77(8) in 2024) have advanced global commitments by calling for integrated emergency, critical and operative (ECO) care within UHC and health emergency preparedness through 2035.6 7

Philanthropic support is the pillar of social development and social justice, and it takes diverse forms, including financial contributions, in-kind donations, service delivery, technical expertise, faith-based initiatives and advocacy. In the literature, philanthropy is broadly defined as the ‘voluntary financial contribution for the public good without an expectation of return’.8 9 Philanthropic funding has historically been an epitome used to scale up global health initiatives. Its global impact is well documented across multiple domains: in maternal and child health, the Gates Foundation (GF), previously known as the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, has supported innovations and maternal health interventions; in communicable diseases, the Global Fund has driven significant progress against HIV, tuberculosis and malaria; in non-communicable diseases such as cervical cancer, philanthropic giving has catalysed immunisation campaigns and screening programmes.

The expansion of surgical care delivery in LMICs is a critical global health priority, yet financing remains a significant challenge.1 Existing databases like those maintained by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) and the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) Creditor Reporting System (CRS) track global health expenditures and external assistance, providing insights into financial contributions from various donors.10 11 While philanthropy plays a critical role in supporting health systems more broadly, its specific contribution to surgical care has yet to be quantified. Hence, this paper seeks to address a pertinent question: ‘What is the financial contribution of philanthropy to surgical care delivery in LMICs?’

## Methodology

This study combines a qualitative and a quantitative component to examine the magnitude of philanthropic contributions in financing surgical care. We conducted a semistructured narrative review of peer-reviewed and grey literature to analyse key concepts, donors and philanthropic organisations, followed by a thematic analysis. We then used the OECD CRS to quantify philanthropic contributions to surgical projects.12

### Qualitative analysis

In the qualitative analysis, a narrative review was conducted with the aim to analyse the roles of philanthropic organisations in financing the expansion of surgical care in LMICs. The review was conducted through an advanced PubMed search, using a keyword search that includes terms such as ‘surgery’, ‘operative’, ‘anesthesia’, ‘blood’, ‘cancer’, ‘cardiac’, ‘cesarean’, ‘obstetric fistula’, ‘neurosurgery’ and ‘trauma’, with the complete PubMed search strategy provided in online supplemental appendix I. Articles from this PubMed search were screened using the eligibility criteria outlined in table 1. The filtered articles then informed a manual targeted search that incorporated additional peer-reviewed articles and grey literature (eg, financial statements, annual reports, organisation websites), as these sources provide credible and detailed information about the bibliographies of philanthropic donors and organisations. Recognising the growing policy interest and academic focus on global surgery over the past decade, the review included publications from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2024, thereby including the years preceding LCoGS. Surgical projects and organisations were considered in scope if they provided full descriptions of their aims, implementation strategies and outcomes on surgical research, delivery and/or advocacy efforts; those lacking such detail were excluded.

## Results

### Qualitative narrative review

The initial PubMed search yielded 540 articles. After removing duplicates and non-English publications, 403 articles remained for screening. Based on title and abstract review applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 47 articles were included for full review. In addition, a targeted search identified 18 more sources, comprising 7 peer-reviewed articles, 8 annual reports and 3 financial statements from philanthropic organisations, bringing the total number of articles included to 65. Figure 1 shows a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA)-style flow diagram outlining the selection of articles included for the narrative review. We identified four themes: (1) general overview of philanthropy, (2) mode of engagement, (3) recipient channels for implementation and (4) facilitators and barriers of philanthropy.

### Overview of philanthropy

Philanthropy plays a crucial role in global health by filling critical financial gaps through partnerships and collaboration on various social causes. Philanthropic contributions are often discretionary and non-contractual, allowing resources to be directed to emerging needs worldwide. Funding originates from individuals, families and corporations, with only limited involvement from governments.13 Most resources are distributed through grantmaking, accounting for up to 75% of financial support, requiring an application process, while gifting relies on the interests and inclinations of philanthropic entities.14 At the global level, philanthropic donors and organisations are highly concentrated in high-income countries (HIC), which account for roughly 95% of cross-border giving and amounting to an estimated $70 billion 2023 Global Philanthropy Tracker.14 Beyond institutional giving, individual donors are estimated to be the largest source of donations worldwide, contributing about $770 billion in monetary donations annually.13

### Mode of engagement in philanthropic giving

Recent developments highlight that philanthropic engagement is no longer limited to traditional single-donor models, but has expanded into more diverse models and modes of participation.13 15

#### Philanthropic giving in partnership with multilaterals

More established philanthropic entities often collaborate with multilateral organisations by contributing to multidonor trust funds. Voluntary contributions to the WHO are largely dominated by philanthropic entities based in HIC, with major private foundations such as the Gates Foundation consistently ranking among WHO’s top three donors globally.16 17 Other philanthropic donors also hold seats on the regulatory boards and act as technical advisors for initiatives. For example, the Global Financing Facility (GFF), a World Bank Group (WBG) initiative that strengthens health financing for women, children and adolescents, pools funds through the GFF Trust Fund Committee.1820 Since 2015, 17 donors (including Gates Foundation and Merck Sharp and Dohme for Mothers) have contributed approximately $2.6 billion to support health initiatives including safe caesarean sections and neonatal resuscitation.21

#### Corporate foundations in corporate social responsibility

Corporate foundations direct profits towards philanthropy reflecting their values and global goals. While this structure can subject them to fluctuations tied to corporate performance, it also enables more flexible alignment of philanthropic capital with emerging global health challenges when compared with other forms of external assistance. In the USA, corporate foundations account for up to one-eighth of private sector philanthropic contributions, highlighting their instrumental role in the financing landscape of global health.22 The European Union, while varying by country, also uses regulatory frameworks that require CSR reporting, indirectly promoting philanthropy as part of social responsibility efforts.23 Corporate foundations have an international imprint that has been visible in surgical research for LMICs, illustrated by initiatives such as the General Electric (GE) Foundation’s Safe Surgery 2020, which directed $25 million towards reducing perioperative mortality and broader surgical system strengthening in Ethiopia, Tanzania and Cambodia.24

#### Domestic philanthropy within LMICs

Domestic philanthropy in LMICs is shifting from dependence on external donors to greater self-sufficiency with local resources. Countries such as India, China and Mexico were seen to have leveraged domestic resources, which has significantly surpassed international inflows.25 Non-profit private organisations sustain domestic philanthropy, such as Pakistan’s Indus Hospital & Health Network, which has provided free surgical care in Karachi since 2007 and derives about one-third of its donations from faith-based Zakat giving.

#### Crowdfunding for surgical expenses

Crowdfunding, or crowdsourcing, enables direct transfer of donations to recipients, bypassing the administrative processes required by larger agencies and institutions.2629 The process involves engaging the public who make monetary contributions to fund various causes via online platforms.30 31 The African Inland Church Kijabe Hospital in Kenya uses the online crowdfunding platform, Watsi, to provide medical services to financially vulnerable patients in the region, including surgery and anaesthesia care, directly covering the patients’ medical bills.31 GoFundMe is also used to reduce out-of-pocket health expenditures, including organ transplants,32 orthopaedic surgery33 and thyroid surgery.34

#### Remittances and diaspora philanthropy

Remittances, commonly used to cover medical expenses, include surgical care.19 As described by the WBG, remittances are personal transfers and employee compensation between residents and non-residents of a country, often sent by migrants, known as the diaspora, to support families in their home countries. In 2023, WBG quantified remittances to approximately $656 billion.35 Recently, remittances traditionally directed towards household consumption and the out-of-pocket health expenditures have slowly evolved into more structured forms of collective financing. The shift of diaspora philanthropy can be seen in an initiative of the Dubai Migrants’ Association. The association established the CH Center medical college, which covered direct and indirect costs of cardiac surgery.36 37

### Recipient channels for implementation

Recipient channels are beneficiaries of philanthropic donations and act as implementing partners. A recipient channel is defined by the OECD, encompasses entities that receive and manage development assistance funds. This includes non-profit non-governmental organisations (NGOs) and charities and academic institutions and societies.

#### Non-profit, non-government organisations and charities

NGOs are self-governing entities engaged in humanitarian and development work that play a critical role in channelling philanthropic funds into surgical care delivery and advocacy efforts in LMICs.38 With funding obtained largely through charitable donations and fundraising, surgical NGOs are estimated to provide around 3 million procedures annually, with specialised organisations accounting for up to 80% of operative caseloads in some settings.39 Surgical care in LMICs is often delivered through various charitable platforms that can be broadly classified into two main types: specialised surgical hospitals and temporary surgical platforms.40 Operation Smile, for example, has delivered more than 350 000 cleft lip and palate surgeries since 1982, while fostering sustainable capacity by establishing independent national branches in emerging economies.41 42 Faith-based charities also contribute substantially, providing an estimated up to 44% of healthcare in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA). Mercy Ships, which operates the world’s two largest non-profit hospital ships, has performed about 117 000 free surgical procedures since inception in 1978, including cleft lip and palate repair, cataract removal, tumour resection, burn reconstruction and orthopaedic surgeries, while partnering with the African Union Development Agency (AUDA-NEPAD) to strengthen regional surgical care.43 44

45

#### Academic institutions and societies

Philanthropic organisations have been instrumental in advancing surgical research and initiatives that align with global development goals. For instance, a notable example by the Wellcome Trust is the $50 million Wellcome Leap Surgery: Assess, Validate, Expand (SAVE) programme launched in 2022, which focuses on research, training and capacity building in Ghana, Nigeria and India. SAVE provides educational models for surgical skills, trains non-physician practitioners to perform elective laparoscopic abdominal surgery and focuses on shortening surgical training duration through advanced teaching methodologies.46 Similarly, private foundations such as the Kletjian Foundation have played pivotal roles in catalysing progress in global surgery, notably through their endowment for surgical research since the LCoGS for the Program in Global Surgery and Social Change at Harvard Medical School, which catalysed recognition of global surgery and established key indicators to evaluate surgical systems worldwide.4749

### Facilitators and barriers to effective philanthropic engagement

#### Facilitators

Philanthropy has been widely studied for its role and underlying mechanisms in driving social initiatives.5052 Philanthropic organisations can take higher financial risks in seeding research and innovations, not confined to the budgetary constraints of fiscal space.52 As compared with the bureaucracies and contractual bipartisan agreements, philanthropy also possesses greater flexibility to respond to acute disasters, evident during the COVID-19 pandemic and in conflict-affected settings such as Somalia, where financial flows are disrupted by violence, terrorism and international sanctions.53 Legal and regulatory reforms that establish transparent governance, minimise bureaucratic barriers to cross-border engagement and introduce fiscal incentives, such as tax benefits for corporate and individual contributions, are essential to enabling philanthropy to effectively support surgical initiatives in LMICs.54

#### Barriers

However, several factors hinder effective philanthropic engagement in LMICs. First, the weak policy environments and limited regulatory frameworks that neither align with global standards nor incentivise giving have inhibited the cross-border flow of resources.53 55 Next, the absence of robust disclosure requirements regarding philanthropic operations, decision-making and impact complicates stakeholders’ ability to assess effectiveness, opening space for misallocation and eroding public trust.55 56 Additionally, declines in philanthropic contributions, alongside reductions in official development assistance, raise concerns about the sustainability of investments in key health priorities. The diversion of resources during the COVID-19 pandemic, for example, shifted funding away from surgical care.5760 Finally, donor dependency is particularly concerning in LMICs, where health systems remain heavily reliant on support for surgical workforce training, essential equipment and service delivery. For example, according to a comprehensive nationwide survey of all health facilities performing operations in Sierra Leone in 2012, private, non-profit facilities performed 54.0% of operations, compared with 39.6% by governmental facilities and 6.4% by private for-profit facilities.61

### Quantitative data analysis

#### Overview

We identified 10 philanthropic organisations in the OECD CRS database that contributed $124.8 million to surgical care from 2014 to 2022. The detailed breakdown of philanthropic donors, including individual disbursement amounts by project category, is provided in online supplemental appendix III. The UBS Optimus Foundation emerged as the largest donor overall. Philanthropic funding for surgical care peaked dramatically in 2019, driven mainly by the UBS Optimus Foundation and the Gates Foundation, before declining sharply in subsequent years as shown in figure 2. UBS Optimus Foundation emerged as the highest donor overall (52.1% of total funding, $65.7 million), with most of its funds going towards paediatric surgery. Following closely to the UBS Optimus Foundation are the Wellcome Trust and the GF, contributing 17.2% ($21.7 million) and 15.5% ($19.5 million), respectively. GF demonstrated the most consistent giving across the study period of 2014–2022, with annual contributions to surgical care ranging from $360 000 to $6.1 million (figure 3), supporting projects such as safe caesarean sections, improving outcomes for postpartum haemorrhage and addressing obstetric fistulas.

*Figure 2: Trends of philanthropic disbursements for surgical care from 2014 to 2022, OECD CRS. OECD CRS, Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development Creditor Reporting System.*

*Figure 3: Proportion of philanthropic disbursements for surgical care from 2014 to 2022, OECD CRS. OECD CRS, Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development Creditor Reporting System.*

#### Recipient regional distribution

Of the total funding earmarked for specific World Bank regions, East Asia and the Pacific received the largest amount of general philanthropic funding at $38 million (30.5%) from 2014 to 2022. China received the greatest amount of philanthropic funding in the East Asia and Pacific region with $37.7 million (online supplemental appendix VI). SSA received the second largest proportion of philanthropic funding at 22.1% ($27.6 million), with Ethiopia gaining the highest amount at $7.4 million. Latin America and the Caribbean received the lowest share of philanthropic disbursements over the study period relative to SSA, South Asia and East Asia.

#### Subspecialties and project categories

Funding was allocated across four project categories (online supplemental appendix IV) and eight surgical subspecialties (online supplemental appendix V). Paediatric surgery received the largest allocation at $49.1 million (95.3% from UBS Optimus Foundation). Disbursements from GF covered a wide range of specialties, from system-level support, such as oxygen and blood supply systems, to surgical education, to various single-specialty programmes. Wellcome Trust displayed a strong focus on critical care, where $6.7 million (31%) of its funds were allocated towards supporting research and innovation in intensive care services to reduce mortality. Other specialties supported include $5.2 million to ophthalmology and $5.1 million to orthopaedics. In contrast, UBS and Conrad Hilton Foundation showed concentrated programmatic interests, namely paediatric surgery and ophthalmology, respectively.

#### Recipient channels

From 2014 to 2022, recipients of philanthropic giving include international NGOs 40% ($50.1 million), LMIC NGOs 30% ($37.4 million), academic partnerships 28% ($35 million) and the private sector 3% ($3.5 million). Online supplemental appendix VII provides a visual representation of the proportion of development assistance by philanthropic organisation allocated to recipient groups. Notably, Wellcome Trust disbursed the majority of its funds to academic institutions, with the highest amount ($20.7 million) going towards universities and research institutions. Additionally, UBS Optimus, Oak Foundation and Conrad Hilton Foundation showed a strong preference for channelling their funds towards NGOs, from a range of 97%–100%. GF was unique in engaging the private sector in addition to NGOs and academia, representing a broader structural flexibility.

## Discussion

### Underfunding in global surgery

Despite surgery’s critical role in addressing nearly one-third of the global disease burden, funding for global surgical care and research remains disproportionately low.1 While private philanthropy contributed approximately $11 billion to health and population initiatives in 2022, representing 5% of total development assistance, only 47% of these funds targeted health-related programmes, and a mere $124.8 million (average of $13.9 million per year) was allocated to surgical initiatives according to this study. Similarly to other studies, global surgery accounted for just 0.8% ($0.03 billion) of surgical research investment between 2016 and 2020, making it the least funded area.62 Historical US data reflect this trend, with NIH and USAID dedicating less than 1% of their budgets to surgical care, primarily obstetric fistula, over two decades.22

### Targeted focus on subspecialties and specific regions

Private philanthropy often fills critical gaps through global health partnerships on health priorities, yet support remains concentrated in elective subspecialties and select regions. In our study, Latin America and the Caribbean received substantially less philanthropic support than SSA despite both being LMICs. Between 2008 and 2013 in another study by Gutnik et al, 160 charitable organisations across five HICs spent $3.0 billion on global surgery, approximately 80.8% from the USA, with most directed to ophthalmology (49%) and cleft lip and palate (26%).63 Surgical NGOs focus where perceived need is greatest; the most commonly served countries were within South Asian and SSA, with African nations prominently represented.39 64 Strategic partner identification in LMICs is essential to align donor–recipient missions with national surgical priorities; mapping giving trends to identify subspecialty entry points and deploying evidence-based advocacy can strengthen national surgical provision, sustain targeted engagement and minimise parallel systems and siloed efforts.

### Non-financial contributions to global surgery

Philanthropic contributions towards surgical initiatives also come in the form of in-kind donation of surgical equipment, volunteerism in short-term surgical missions and the establishment of surgical specialised hospitals.40 65 Surgical delivery occurs via specialised hospitals and temporary platforms; short-term missions, while sometimes the only option, generally yield poorer outcomes and are not cost-effective, self-contained temporary platforms show promise on limited evidence, and specialised hospitals provide effective, potentially sustainable care though cost-effectiveness metrics are scarce.40

### Strengths and weaknesses of this study

This paper aimed to broadly explore the financial contributions of philanthropy to surgical care delivery. The narrative review captured diverse initiatives to expand surgical care in LMICs, but providing a comprehensive list of every philanthropic organisation was beyond the scope of this study, as we did not aim to enumerate every philanthropic organisation in PubMed-indexed literature. As a result, smaller or less established charities are under-represented, and contributions from anonymous donors, in-kind support, individual, anonymous and undocumented funding are difficult to quantify systematically. We used the OECD CRS to quantify philanthropic contributions to surgical projects because it offers the most comprehensive, publicly available dataset on external aid, taking into account bilateral, multilateral and philanthropic donors, in order to ensure methodological coherency and consistency with other analyses in this series (eg, multilateral partnerships and bilateral assistance). While OECD CRS aims to advance transparency in global development financing, it does not capture all philanthropic flows: individual donations are generally excluded unless aggregated by NGOs or foundations, and some financial resources are aggregated under ‘mixed’ or ‘unspecified’ country or region groups, constraining attribution in this analysis. Additionally, loose definition of ‘surgery’, and combined with the lack of a standardised classification system limits keyword-based identification, risking omission of some proportion of funding relevant to global surgery.

## Conclusion

Global surgery remains chronically underfunded despite its substantial burden of disease, highlighting the importance of renewed investment more urgently in light of evolving international foreign aid policies. Philanthropy often focuses resources where perceived need is greatest and can directly close financial gaps by seeding and catalysing surgical systems, making it a pivotal lever for advancing the expansion of access to surgical care LMICs. Philanthropic actors, including private and corporate foundations, individual donors, NGOs and the private sector, form an intersecting financing ecosystem that addresses critical gaps: remittances, crowdfunding and non-profit private hospital models help defray direct surgical costs; foundations channel gifts and grants through NGOs, academic institutions and professional societies; the private sector advances research and innovation; and non-profit hospital models may provide sustainable financing pathways. Although modest in scale as compared with other external aid mechanisms, philanthropy has the potential to seed and catalyse surgical systems, advancing the expansion of access to surgical care LMICs.

# Analysis of bilateral development assistance for surgery in low- and middle-income countries: trends, challenges and opportunities

**Authors:** Simon Fabry; Gabriella Yael Hyman; Nardos Getachew Bulfeta; Desmond T Jumbam; John E Varallo; Kee B Park

**Affiliations:** 1Harvard Medical School Program in Global Surgery and Social Change, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 2Department of Global Health and Social Medicine, Harvard Medical School Program in Global Surgery and Social Change, Boston, Massachusetts, USA | 3Department of Surgery, University of the Witwatersrand Johannesburg Faculty of Health Sciences, Johannesburg, South Africa | 4Global Health Unfiltered, Accra, Ghana | 5Women’s Health, Global Surgery Foundation, Geneva, Switzerland

## Abstract

Surgical care in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) remains underfunded despite representing a significant portion of the Global Burden of Disease. Understanding bilateral development assistance for surgery is crucial to address this disparity.

We conducted a narrative review and quantitative analysis of bilateral development assistance for surgery in LMICs from 2014 to 2022 using data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development Creditor Reporting System. Surgical projects were identified through keyword search. We report funding trends, key actors, project classifications, implementation channels and regional distribution, and examine trends through thematic analysis of key characteristics of bilateral aid.

Between 2014 and 2022, US$2.73 billion was disbursed to surgical projects. Surgical funding decreased as a proportion of total bilateral development assistance for health (DAH), from 2.13% in 2014 to 1.32% in 2022. Key donors were Canada, the USA, Australia, Italy and Korea. Obstetrics and gynaecology received the most funding among surgical subspecialties. Non-governmental organisations were the primary implementation channels (51.4%), which could undermine public sector development by bypassing national health systems, perpetuating fragmentation and limiting governments’ capacity to sustain surgical services independently. Sub-Saharan Africa was the principal recipient region, securing 55.17% of disbursements.

Despite increasing commitments, surgical care remains underfunded, with an overall 1.84% share of bilateral DAH. Contributing factors include limited expressed public sector demand and absorption capacity in recipient countries, donor disbursement practices tied to performance indicators and shifting donor priorities. Recipient countries can enhance funding utilisation and donor attraction by strengthening national surgical plans, improving health system capacity, engaging stakeholders collaboratively, advocating for balanced funding across specialties and exploring innovative financing mechanisms. Addressing these challenges is essential to optimising surgical care funding and improving health outcomes in LMICs.

## WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

- Bilateral aid plays a key role in supporting health-related sustainable development goals in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Despite the increasing attention to surgical systems strengthening in LMICs, bilateral assistance to surgical systems remains unquantified.

## WHAT THIS STUDY ADDS

- Drawing from databases that track bilateral development assistance for health, we quantified bilateral aid to surgical care in LMICs from 2014 to 2022. Surgical care is underfunded as a proportion of total bilateral assistance to health. The landscape of bilateral donors which disburse to surgical care shows a distributed donor base compared with the handful of donors that dominate the bilateral aid to health portfolio. Notably, a subset of these donors allocated a substantial share of their bilateral aid portfolios to surgical care, suggesting differential prioritisation across the donor landscape.

## HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

- The underfunding of surgical care within bilateral aid portfolios strengthens the case for explicit surgical care targets in donor health strategies, similar to commitments that exist for other domains. The variation in donor prioritisation raises important questions about what drives donor decision-making in surgical aid allocation, from diplomatic relationships and recipient country advocacy to health securitisation, and disease burden data.

## Introduction

In global health discourse, certain disease areas frequently dominate the agenda—infectious diseases, reproductive, maternal, neonatal and child health (RMNCH), trauma, and non-communicable diseases (NCDs).1 Donors and international organisations design their strategies and allocate funding with these priorities in mind, principally guided by the objectives of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).2 3

It might be assumed that surgery largely falls under the NCDs umbrella,4 which account for an estimated 74% of deaths worldwide. This figure rises to 77% of the total and 86% of premature deaths in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs).5 However, surgery transcends this single category and is vital for addressing a multitude of pressing global health challenges—from reducing high mortality rates in RMNCH to managing complications of infectious diseases to containing the escalating burden of injuries and trauma.6

In 2015, the Lancet Commission on Global Surgery reported that 5 billion people lack access to safe and affordable surgical and anaesthesia care, highlighting profound global disparities that disproportionately affect LMICs.7 Scholarly works have emphasised that surgical care is essential to achieving universal health coverage (UHC),8 and multilateral organisations such as the WHO have increasingly recognised the importance of surgical and anaesthesia care in various resolutions and frameworks,9 fueling the global surgery movement. Consequently, global health leaders have intensified efforts to bolster surgical capacities in LMICs, especially as UHC and donor priorities have become central to global health discussions.10 11

Despite the increasing acknowledgement of the importance of surgical care, securing funding for it remains a significant challenge.12 Donor reluctance to fund NCDs has been attributed to several factors: the absence of disease transmissibility, high intervention costs, inadequate infrastructure, and the complexity and delayed measurability of outcomes.13 These challenges are equally, if not more, pertinent to the field of surgery, which is often overlooked as an integral component of the continuum of care.14

The development of National Surgical Plans (NSPs) has been crucial in attracting funding for surgery15 16 by facilitating potential donor cooperation and integrating surgical care into broader national health policies.17 While multiple LMICs are in various stages of NSP development and implementation,1821 most of these efforts remain underfunded and require further support to become operational.12 To bolster donor attraction and ownership, the Pan-African Surgical Healthcare Forum has added the development of national health insurance schemes and improvements in infrastructure and equipment for surgical care as recommendations to their consensus statement. Additionally, participating ministries of health consented to establish a budget line for surgical and anaesthesia care, stating that NSPs alone would not be sufficient in achieving surgical system integration or attracting further funding.22

As part of a broader series on funding avenues for surgery, this study concentrates on bilateral aid. Bilateral development assistance for health (DAH) refers to financial and technical support provided directly by a donor country’s government to a recipient country via various implementation channels aimed at improving health outcomes and strengthening health systems.23 To fully address the challenges that recipient countries face when seeking bilateral assistance for surgery, it is necessary to understand the current landscape. Our study aims to equip LMICs with the knowledge and strategies needed to navigate this vital funding source to finance their NSPs. It presents evidence on characteristics, opportunities, and barriers of bilateral aid and quantifies bilateral assistance to surgical care over the past decade. Hence, our research question is as follows: Based on data from 2014 to 2022, what lessons can be learnt from the landscape, trends and patterns of bilateral assistance to LMICs for surgical care?

## Methods

This study consists of quantitative analysis and narrative review of literature.

### Data sources and preparation

We conducted a quantitative data analysis of DAH using two primary databases: the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) Financing Global Health Database24 and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) Creditor Reporting System (CRS) database.25 These two databases are publicly available, methodologically rigorous and transparent, and collect data from multiple sources to compile evidence on development assistance. The list of bilateral donors included in our analysis is listed in online supplemental appendix IA.

Data analysis was performed using R Studio statistical software R V.24.04.02.26

#### IHME Financing Global Health Database

The IHME database provided an overview of bilateral aid trends from 2014 to 2022, including data on donor sources, funding channels and recipient regions. The IHME employs various methodologies to impute missing data,27 and missing data in this dataset was <5%. After removing duplicates, we aggregated the data to focus exclusively on bilateral channels. Custom health focus areas relevant to surgical conditions were identified: NCDs (excluding mental health and tobacco control), maternal and child health (MCH) (including neonatal care and excluding vaccine programmes) and sector-wide approaches (SWAps, excluding pandemic preparedness programmes). The cleaning and aggregation of IHME data offered an overview of bilateral aid trends for the years 2014–2022 revealing important data on sources, funding channels and recipient regions. Additionally, for the years 2014–2022, we were able to extract bilateral aid data for the custom health focus areas relevant to our analysis.

#### OECD CRS database

The OECD CRS28 collects data from members of the Development Assistance Committee (DAC), non-DAC member states, multilateral organisations and philanthropy, allowing uniform comparison across organisations to address our main research question. It offers detailed project-level information, including project titles, descriptions, implementing entities and financial commitments and disbursements. The database is updated at least twice a year, in April and December to report provisional and completed values of the preceding year, respectively.29 The study used the June 2024 version, which was the most complete version for the latest year (2022) we reported, to avoid provisional data. Data preparation included merging data for the years 2014–2022 and excluding data with sector codes other than the health-related DAC sector codes (DAC3 codes: 120, 121, 122, 123 and 130). We excluded data not reported as bilateral and retained the ‘USD Disbursement Deflated’ column as our primary financial measure.

#### Identification of surgical projects

Data extraction of surgical projects involved a comprehensive keyword search using terms in English, French and Spanish that were widely associated with surgery, including, but not limited to, ‘cirugía’, ‘operación’, ‘quirúrgico’, ‘pediátrico’, ‘oncológico’, ‘oxígeno’, ‘sangre’, ‘anestesia’ and ‘anestesiología’. This method is adopted from the IHME method to comprehensively search the project descriptions in the CRS database, which is reported in various languages.27 Full keywords are detailed in online supplemental appendix IB.

Inclusion criteria encompassed projects with surgical aspects, surgical system integration initiatives, emergency, critical and operative care, surgical equipment and infrastructure, blood supply and transfusion services, digital health, telemedicine, perioperative services and capacity building (including non-specialist surgical training). Exclusion criteria included projects exclusively on infectious diseases without addressing surgical complications, non-surgical RMNCH, research in high-income countries, general public health initiatives without a surgical focus, pharmaceutical research and development, and projects without clear relevance to surgical care (see online supplemental appendix IC). The parent and child codes have been outlined in online supplemental appendix ID. Projects that have keywords that fit multiple surgical specialty categories were classified as ‘Multispecialty Programs’.

We quantified total bilateral aid for the study period, described trends in disbursements, key actors, preference of implementation channels, and regional distribution. All values are expressed in 2022 USD values. Full details of quantitative analysis are provided in online supplemental appendix IE.

### Narrative review

To further assess the role of bilateral aid in surgical care and how those characteristics influence disbursement trends and other quantitative findings, we conducted a narrative review with thematic analysis. Literature search was performed on MEDLINE and Google Scholar using a combination of keywords (see online supplemental appendix II). The review focused on themes related to accessing bilateral assistance for surgery: facilitators, barriers and unique attributes in comparison to other funding channels. Findings are presented as comparative advantages and disadvantages to inform strategies for strengthening bilateral aid flows to surgical care in LMICs.

Title and abstract screening was performed independently by two authors (SF and GYH), with discrepancies resolved through consultation with NB. Eligibility criteria (table 1) guided the selection of titles and abstracts, after which full texts of qualifying articles were retrieved and reviewed. While surgical care is cross-cutting across various domains, for the majority of global health discourse over the past two decades, surgically treatable conditions such as cancer, cardiovascular and neurovascular diseases have been placed under the NCDs category per the Global Burden of Disease (GBD). NCDs were therefore in our inclusion criteria. The GBD category ‘Injuries’ was not included due to multiple humanitarian and disaster relief aid, which is distinct from development aid and was excluded from our quantitative analysis on the same basis. Once the final set of relevant documents was established, SF undertook inductive coding at the paragraph level in Microsoft Word to categorise content characterising governance, capacity and distinguishing features of bilateral aid. Emerging codes were then reviewed collaboratively by authors and consolidated into four overarching themes which formed the basis for synthesising the findings. | Grant | Transfers in cash or in kind for which no legal debt is incurred by the recipient.69 |

## Results

### Bilateral assistance for health 2014–2023

#### Trends in disbursements

In 2022, governments provided US$53.8 billion in DAH, constituting roughly 76% of all DAH recorded (US$71.1 billion). Governmental aid included US$20.3 billion in core contributions to multilateral organisations, primarily GAVI and the Global Fund, and an additional US$2.26 billion in core contributions to non-governmental organisations (NGOs). The remaining US$27.8 billion, about 39.1% of all DAH, was identified as bilateral aid. This represents a 109.8% increase in bilateral disbursements from 2014 (US$13.25 billion), where bilateral assistance represented a significantly lower 30.7% of total DAH (US$43.17 billion). Bilateral aid from 2014 to 2022 accounted for 41% of DAH.

#### Key actors

Bilateral aid is driven by several key donor countries; from 2014 to 2022, the USA was the largest contributor, providing over US$75.7 billion in DAH, approximately 51% of all bilateral assistance (US$147.8 billion). Germany contributed US$14.6 billion and the UK provided US$10.7 billion. Other significant donors included Japan (US$7.8 billion), France (US$5.5 billion) and Canada (US$5.6 billion). In total, more than 81% of all bilateral assistance was provided by these six donors. China, the only emerging donor included in the IHME database, ranked fifth with US$6.25 billion in disbursements.

#### Implementation channels

In 2022, a considerable portion, 36%, was directed at public sector entities, primarily recipient governments. Multilateral organisations channelled 28% bilateral aid for earmarked projects, while civil society received 16% for specified projects. The involvement of the private sector in the recipient country was evident, with 9%, and academic and research institutions with 5%. Lastly, 2% was allocated to public–private partnerships and networks.

#### Health focus areas

While the IHME Financing Global Health database offers Health Focus Areas (Parent Codes) and Program Areas (Child Codes) to estimate funding for specific diseases, surgery or surgical conditions are not tracked separately.

Analysis of custom aggregates, which exclude non-surgical areas, reveals moderate trends (figure 1). MCH funding fluctuated over the period, peaking at US$1.428 billion in 2019 before declining sharply to US$0.752 billion in 2021, with a slight recovery to US$0.994 billion in 2022. NCD funding showed a general upward trend, increasing from US$0.074 billion in 2014 to US$0.187 billion in 2022, despite some year-to-year variations. SWAps funding demonstrated the highest overall levels and relative stability, ranging from US$1.120 billion to US$1.749 billion, with projected funding of US$1.611 billion for 2022. In comparison, funding for infectious diseases rose steadily from US$10.19 billion in 2014 to US$25.03 billion in 2022.

### Bilateral assistance for surgery, 2014–2022

In our analysis of OECD CRS data from 2014 to 2022, a total of 3153 surgical projects were identified, involving 39 bilateral donors (list included in the online supplemental appendix) and 129 recipient countries across 6 World Bank regions.

#### Trends in disbursements

Bilateral disbursement to surgical care totalled US$2.73 billion in the study period. Analysis revealed significant fluctuations in bilateral funding (see online supplemental appendix III, figure i) with annual values ranging from US$192 million to US$440 million. While overall health sector disbursements increased substantially, surgical project funding represented 1.84%, a declining fraction of total bilateral DAH, dropping from 2.1% in 2014 to 1.32% in 2022.

#### Key actors

Certain countries emerged as key donors in surgical funding (figure 2), and their contributions were analysed relative to their total bilateral DAH. Canada contributed US$596.1 million to surgical projects, representing 16.72% of its total bilateral DAH, with high yearly variability peaking at 39.12% in 2017. The United States provided US$582.5 million to surgical projects, with surgical funding representing 0.78% of its total bilateral DAH, ranging from 0.31% to 1.87% over the years. Australia’s disbursement to surgical projects was US$241.9 million, accounting for 8.6% of its total bilateral DAH. Italy’s total disbursement to surgical projects was US$207 million. Surgical funding accounted for 17.56% of Italy’s total bilateral DAH, peaking at 36.67% in 2019. Korea’s disbursement to surgical projects was US$191 million, accounting for 6.81% of its total bilateral DAH. The United Arab Emirates (UAE) disbursed US$97.7 million to surgical projects, with surgical funding constituting 9.37% of its total bilateral DAH.

#### Project classification and funding allocation

#### Subspecialties

The analysis of funding allocation to surgical subspecialties revealed distinct patterns. Obstetrics and gynaecology emerged as the most funded single specialty domain, with annual disbursements ranging between US$17.7 million and US$118.3 million. Ophthalmology received significant funding, often in the range of US$3.5–US$25.7 million per year. Orthopaedics and trauma care secured the third-largest share, receiving between US$2 and US$21 million annually, often associated with integrated primary healthcare initiatives or humanitarian projects in conflict or disaster areas. Paediatric surgery has gained increasing attention over the years, with disbursements rising from less than US$1 million in 2015 to more than US$10 million in recent years. Other surgical specialties, such as general surgery, neurosurgery, and urology, received smaller but steady allocations, typically under US$5 million annually.

#### Infrastructure and equipment

Funding for infrastructure and equipment received the highest allocations among all categories, ranging from US$99.8 million to US$222.3 million annually. This focus underscores the recognition of inadequate surgical facilities and medical equipment as major barriers to surgical care in LMICs30 and easily trackable and measurable outcomes for donors. Investments in infrastructure include constructing and equipping hospitals, upgrading operating rooms, and enhancing supply chain management systems.

### Implementation channels

When examining the implementation channels for surgical funding within the study period, NGOs received the largest share at 51.4%, highlighting the significant role of NGOs in implementing surgical system development and capacity building in LMICs. Public Sector Entities received 31.72% of funding directly, facilitating direct support for national health systems. Universities and Research Institutions accounted for 5.42% of funding, reflecting contributions to academic collaborations, training, and research initiatives. Multilateral entities including the UN channelled only 6.83% of funds (figure 3).
